U.S. stocks plunged Friday as a deepening sell-off in artificial intelligence companies sent Wall Street toward its worst weekly performance in more than a year, with investors increasingly concerned about technology valuations and the prospect of higher interest rates.

The Nasdaq Composite tumbled more than 5% in late afternoon trading, erasing its gains for 2026. The S&P 500 dropped 3.5%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.7%. Both the Dow and S&P 500 slipped into correction territory, trading more than 10% below their October record highs.

The S&P 500 was on track for its seventh consecutive losing session, marking its longest losing streak since February 2020, when the emergence of the COVID-19 pandemic rattled global financial markets.

All three major indexes were headed toward their worst weekly percentage losses since April 2025, when President Donald Trump's sweeping tariff announcement triggered a global market downturn. The Dow had already lost approximately 6.2% this week through Thursday's close.

Technology stocks were at the center of Friday's retreat, as the highly anticipated market debut of artificial intelligence developer Anthropic failed to restore confidence in a sector that had powered much of Wall Street's rally this year.

The company behind the Claude chatbot raised approximately $81 billion in its initial public offering on Thursday, surpassing SpaceX to become the largest IPO in history. Anthropic priced its shares at $83 and initially surged more than 30% when trading began. However, the stock surrendered much of those gains before Thursday's closing bell and continued falling Friday.

The disappointing performance compounded concerns about whether the enormous amounts of money flowing into AI companies and infrastructure can generate sufficient returns to justify their valuations.

Semiconductor manufacturers suffered some of Friday's heaviest losses. Nvidia shares plunged approximately 12%, while Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom and Micron Technology also recorded double-digit declines during the session.

Amazon and Meta Platforms also came under pressure, while AI cloud infrastructure providers CoreWeave and Nebius recorded substantial losses. Companies benefiting indirectly from the expansion of AI infrastructure were also affected. Caterpillar shares declined amid concerns that a slowdown in data center investment could weaken demand for power generation equipment.

The technology rout spread internationally, with Japan's Nikkei and South Korea's Kospi both falling more than 5%. Adding to Wall Street's challenges were growing expectations that the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates again as inflation remains stubbornly elevated.

Amazon is Anthropic's biggest shareholder. It holds about 1.94 billion non-voting shares, or 14.6%, after investing roughly $18 billion, Fortune reported from the final prospectus. At Anthropic's $97.17 close, Amazon's stake is worth about $188 billion, roughly 6.8% of Amazon's $2.78 trillion market value on GuruFocus. That cuts both ways, because each $1 move in Anthropic's shares changes the stake by about $1.9 billion and can whipsaw reported net income. The GuruFocus chart shows a GF Score of 93/100, signaling strong profitability and momentum with a balance sheet that is solid rather than spotless. GF Value is $259.88, so the shares trade about 1% below it, fairly valued. The bull case is already in the price. The next test is whether AWS growth in the fourth quarter shows the $110 billion commitment turning into recognized revenue.

Anthropic (NASDAQ:ANT) closed its first trading day at $97.17 at 4:00 p.m. ET on November 19, up 17.07% from its $83 IPO price on Nasdaq. The ride was wild. The first trade crossed at $111.50 at 11:48 a.m. ET, ran to $114.99 a minute later, then sank to $92.72 by 1:18 p.m. as the wider market slid 2%. Roughly 832 million shares changed hands on day one.

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 3 Warning Signs with NVDA.

Is ANT fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

The deal is the largest on record. Anthropic sold 980 million Class A shares for $81.34 billion in gross proceeds after pricing above its $70 to $78 range. A separate $26 billion non-voting placement at $83 brought in Google and Nvidia at about $10 billion each, AMD at $2.5 billion, Broadcom, Micron and Microsoft at about $1 billion each, and TSMC at $500 million. Amazon holds 14.6% and Google 13.4% after the offering, per the final prospectus. Cloud marketplaces generated about 44% of Anthropic's revenue in the first nine months of 2026, according to Fortune, a reminder of how tightly its sales run through partners that are also rivals.

At the close, GuruFocus puts Anthropic's market value at $1.28 trillion. The GuruFocus chart shows a GF Score of just 10/100, which says the listing has almost no public track record of profitability and only middling balance-sheet strength to grade yet, so the score flags data risk more than business quality. Supply is the next test. Up to 315 million insider shares were eligible to sell from day one, and a further 303 million could unlock on December 15. A record pop does not set a floor, and the first quarterly report will decide whether $1.28 trillion is a starting point or a peak.

title: Is Apple Stock Increasing Your Market Risk?

Is Apple Stock Increasing Your Market Risk?

Today's big story: Will 2027 Be A 2022 Repeat For Stocks?

You may already own Apple (AAPL) or be preparing to buy it, likely alongside money that already tracks the S&P 500. Apple closed trading on November 19, 2026, with a market value of about $5.1 trillion. At that size, the company's daily moves affect your entire account, not just the individual shares you hold. So when the index slides, does Apple drag the rest of your money down with it?

Apple Has Fallen Less On The Market's Down Days

Not as much as the index does. Over the past year through November 19, 2026, a $10,000 position in Apple lost about $31 on the average day the S&P 500 fell. The same amount invested in the index lost about $64 on those days. On the average up day, the Apple holding gained about $52, against about $67 for the index. On those averages, Apple kept most of the market's gains and took less than half of its losses.

Apple lost about half as much as the index on the market's average down day. But if Apple is a big share of your savings, a bad month still hurts, and selling some after five years of gains could bring a large tax bill. Our partner advisory firm will take your question on a free 30-minute call, by phone or video, with no obligation. Book a free call.

Apple's own swings were wider, though. Its volatility, how far the price tends to swing over a year, was 24.9% over the past year. That compares with 13.9% for the S&P 500. Yet its beta, how far Apple tends to move for every point the index moves, was 0.63. So Apple added swings of its own, and over the past year it moved less than the index for each point the index moved.

Why Apple's Swings Are Likely To Continue

Apple's swings are likely to remain wide because the company relies on one product for more than half of its sales and is paying more to make its devices. The iPhone generated $254 billion of Apple's $479 billion in revenue during fiscal 2026. For the quarter that ended September 26, 2026, Apple reported a gross margin of 47.9%. Management forecast a gross margin of 45% to 46% for the December quarter, mainly because of higher memory costs. The company also expects memory prices to keep rising after December, leaving Apple's profit tied to chip prices it does not set.

Over the past year, Apple's daily moves aligned only loosely with the broader index. The two posted a correlation of 0.35, a metric where 1 means two prices move in step. Over the five years to November 19, 2026, that correlation stood at 0.71. Apple's loose link to the market over the past year may therefore not be its usual pattern.

Cerebras Systems (NASDAQ:CBRS) continued to rebound from its lows, climbing 11% on Nov. 13 after the stock reported soaring revenue and announced a deal with Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT). However, the semiconductor stock is still down more than 40% from its $185 IPO price in May, and more than 70% off its highs.

Cerebras, which makes systems built around its wafer-scale chips the size of an iPad, has thus far been more of a niche provider of high-end artificial intelligence inference (AI) systems with a small customer base. As such, the deal with Microsoft is important, as Cerebras continues to expand its client list, which now includes OpenAI, Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN), and Oracle (NYSE:ORCL). As the company's systems move into the mainstream, it still looks like a good time to buy the stock.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: The Motley Fool.

Surging revenue

In addition to the big deal with Microsoft, Cerebras also addressed rumors around OpenAI, which is set to become its largest customer. It noted that it didn't have enough capacity to provide the system behind OpenAI's ultra-fast mode for its latest models, and that this was why its solution wasn't used, not for technical reasons.

Cerebras has a take-or-pay contract with OpenAI worth more than $20 billion for 750 megawatts of capacity, accounted for in its remaining performance obligations (RPOs), which total $26.1 billion as of the end of September. Notably, the Oracle and Microsoft deals were signed after the quarter and are not in that amount. Due to delays, Cerebras may owe OpenAI delay credits, which were deducted from its RPOs.

Despite some hiccups with OpenAI, Cerebras saw its revenue jump 55% to $210.8 million. Its core sales figure, which strips out revenue distortions from customer warrants and pass-through accounting, soared 70% to $230.9 million, topping the $214.7 million consensus, as compiled by LSEG.

Customers continue to prefer renting its systems, leading to its cloud revenue climbing 265% year over year to $141.9 million and its core cloud revenue surging 287% to $144.9 million. Hardware revenue sank 29% year over year to $68.9 million, while core hardware revenue slipped 11% to $86 million.

Gross margins have been an issue for Cerebras. Its core gross margins came in at 41%, up 30 basis points versus a year ago. Core gross margin for its cloud operation was 46.9%, a big improvement from 16.5% a year ago. However, its core hardware gross margin was 31%, down from 50.5% a year ago. The company said this was due to the continued ramp of its manufacturing capabilities and the final shipments of hardware to early customers under special pricing. Its long-term target for hardware gross margins is 60%. Meanwhile, its cloud gross margins were impacted by Cerebras renting back some equipment from a customer.

title: AI Stocks are on Sale: A Generational Buying Opportunity
detail:
AI Stocks are on Sale: A Generational Buying Opportunity
Tracey Ryniec

AMZN
Trade AMZN on Coinbase

What if you could buy Amazon at $6.00 a share? Or Booking at $1.80?

It may seem like a dream to think of buying these two successful, well-known companies at such low share prices. But in 2001, you could.

Amazon DID sell at $6.00 a share in 2001. Booking, then known as Priceline, was $1.80, or split adjusted, $10.35 in 2001.

Yes, it was after the dotcom bubble had burst and had turned into a bust. By 2001, investors had run for the hills and had dumped their Internet stocks.

But if you were an investor willing to jump in and take a chance, with a multi-year time horizon, it became the buying opportunity of a lifetime.

How Do You Know When It's a Buying Opportunity and Not a Trap?

After the Internet boom, there were plenty of companies that went on sale. Many of those were dotcoms like Webvan or Pets.com, which couldn't hold on for a turnaround and ended up bankrupt.

But Amazon and Booking, both also dot-coms, did not fail.

Was their survival just luck or something else?

The 2 Keys to Finding Generational Buying Opportunities

What if an investor could look at certain fundamentals to determine if the company was a buying opportunity and could avoid the Webvans and find the Amazons?

There's no sure thing in investing. There's also no secret screen you can run that will give you only the Amazons during a market sell-off.

But you can stack the odds in your favor by looking at a few key fundamentals.

1) Is the company profitable?

This may seem basic but whether a company has profits, and therefore has earnings, is a key indicator of survival when times get tough.

In 2000, Booking actually lost $0.05 a share, but by 2001, it made $0.01 and never saw negative earnings again. It has grown the earnings every year since. In 2025, Booking made $9.14 per share.

2) Are earnings growing?

In 2022, technology and growth stocks plunged after the Federal Reserve sharply raised interest rates to cool the economy and inflation. This created a generational buying opportunity in many technology stocks like Shopify, which fell 86% from its highs in 2021.

In 2021, Shopify made $0.36 per share. But after the Federal Reserve raised rates, Shopify's business took a hit and earnings went negative. In 2022, Shopify lost $0.39.

Still, the company didn't stay down for very long. By 2023, it had turned the earnings around and saw a gain of $0.27. It has grown its earnings by the double digits or better every year since.

This was a buying opportunity in Shopify. Shares are up 368% from the October 2022 lows.

Are AI Stocks a Generational Buying Opportunity?

Despite all the worrying, in November 2026, the AI Revolution doesn't appear to be slowing down. But the stocks have retreated from their highs earlier this year, some dramatically so.

Is this another generational buying opportunity like buying Amazon and Booking in 2001 or Shopify in 2022, or a trap.

CoreWeave has been one of the AI Revolution companies that has sold off on worries about financing of the AI buildout. Shares have plunged 55% in the last three months.

A quick look at its earnings should tell the tale.

CoreWeave saw negative earnings of $1.52 per share in 2025 and the loss is expected to get bigger in 2026, at negative $3.79. Even into 2027, analysts still expect another year of negative earnings of $2.04.

It's going the wrong way on earnings as well. They are sliding instead of growing. This is a red flag.
